content: Medication reconciliation is a structured process aimed at obtaining a comprehensive and accurate list of a patient’s current home medications. This includes the medication name, dosage, frequency, and route of administration. The process involves comparing this list to the medications ordered during hospital admission, transfer, or discharge to identify and resolve discrepancies, thereby preventing medication errors. A key component of this process is the creation of a Best Possible Medication History (BPMH). Older adults often face challenges in accurately recalling their medications, which can complicate this process. The Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) defines medication reconciliation as the process of creating the most accurate list of all medications a patient is taking. Similarly, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) describes it as identifying the most accurate list of all medications a patient is taking. The Joint Commission emphasizes that a clinician compares the medications a patient should be using (and is actually using) to the new medications ordered for the patient, resolving any discrepancies. Frequency of Reconciliation Errors In inpatient settings, medication errors occur at varying rates: Discrepancies in medication lists have been reported in 17%, 44%, 46%, and 60% of cases. Inappropriate medication choices, as determined by STOPP/START criteria, occur in 48% of cases. A related issue, though not classified as an error, is the increase in medication intensity at hospital discharge. In outpatient settings, the rates of medication discrepancies are even higher, ranging from 44% to 88%. Specific errors identified in inpatient studies include: Discrepancies in discharge summaries (34%). Duplicate medications (23%). Extraneous medications (14%). Errors related to medications prescribed for specific indications or diseases (25%). Omission of necessary medications (17%). Frequency of Harm from Reconciliation Errors Studies have documented the clinical impact of medication errors, though it remains unclear how many of these issues could be prevented through successful medication reconciliation. In one study involving 851 patients with acute coronary syndrome (ACS) or congestive heart failure (CHF), pharmacist-assisted medication reconciliation, combined with low-literacy adherence aids and follow-up calls, revealed: 50.8% of patients experienced clinically significant medication errors. 22.9% of these errors were serious, and 1.8% were life-threatening. 30.3% of patients experienced adverse drug events, while 29.7% had potential adverse events. In another study involving 510 hematology/oncology patients undergoing infusion therapy, student pharmacists identified: At least one medication discrepancy in 88% of patients, which was subsequently corrected in the electronic medical record (EMR). Medication-related problems, such as drug-drug interactions, untreated indications, and adverse drug reactions, in 11.4% of patients. In outpatient settings, discrepancies between patients’ self-reported medication use and medical records have been linked to poor hypertension control in safety-net clinics. Criteria for Identifying Medication Problems One proposed metric for assessing medication reconciliation is the number of unintentional medication discrepancies per patient. This approach requires a trained pharmacist to establish a gold standard, with recommendations to sample 25 patients per month. However, this method has limitations, including unclear criteria for pharmacist assessments and the inability to automate the process using routinely collected clinical data. Pharmacist-led medication reconciliation can take over two hours, whereas physicians in clinical settings may have less than a minute to discuss medications with patients. Specific Criteria for Medication Reconciliation A study conducted at the Washington DC VA hospital proposed specific criteria for medication reconciliation, involving internal medicine residents who participated in bi-monthly educational sessions. The criteria included: Identification of duplicate medications. Identification of extraneous medications, also referred to as one-time, post-acute, or time-limited medications. Discrepancies in discharge summaries. Omission of necessary medications. Grouping medications by indication or disease. Another study at National Jewish Health in Denver focused on an ambulatory practice serving patients with respiratory and related diseases. Over 18 months, the study demonstrated improvements in medication reconciliation processes: Electronic documentation of completed medication reconciliation during clinic visits increased from 9.8% to 91.3%. Medication duplication rates decreased from 4.0% to 2.6%. Significant improvements were observed in addressing missing doses and frequencies. Patients were provided with medication safety handouts, including updated medication lists. Despite these improvements, compliance remained a challenge due to participant resistance, often attributed to the perceived redundancy of the process. Role of Patient Engagement and Understanding Elderly patients often struggle to understand changes in their medication regimens. Low health literacy is a significant factor contributing to medication discrepancies. Role of Regional Health Information Exchanges The use of regional health information exchanges has been proposed to improve medication reconciliation. However, the clinical benefits of these systems remain unproven. A randomized controlled trial found no reduction in adverse drug reactions associated with their use. Public Reporting Medication reconciliation is included in the CMS Electronic Health Record (EHR) Incentive Programs, specifically in the Meaningful Use Stage 1 and the 2017 Modified Stage 2 Meaningful Use Program Requirements. Interventions to Promote Successful Medication Reconciliation Medication reconciliation alone may not be sufficient to prevent hospital readmissions. While it can reduce emergency department visits, its effectiveness in preventing readmissions is limited. Combining medication reconciliation with follow-up phone calls has shown mixed results. Studies suggest that benefits are more likely when multiple, scripted phone calls are made, and patients are encouraged to have their medications on hand during these calls. Multifactorial interventions that include medication reconciliation may be more effective in reducing hospital readmissions.
